text: A shooting star, or [[meteor|meteor]], is a speck of space dust burning up as it rushes into our air. It has nothing to do with real stars.

Most of these specks are smaller than a grain of rice. They hit Earth's [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] at tens of kilometres per second, far faster than any bullet. At that speed, the air in front of them is squeezed and heated so violently that the speck and the air around it glow white-hot. The streak of light lasts a second or so, about 100 km above the ground.

st.reveal: Most shooting stars are specks of space dust, from sand-grain to pea size. They hit our air so fast, tens of kilometres per second, that they heat up and glow about 100 km above you.

sec.t:
Space is sprinkled with dust and grit. Much of it was shed by [[@comets|comets]] as they passed the Sun, and some comes from [[asteroid|asteroids]] bumping together.

On any dark, clear night, you might see a few meteors an hour. But at certain times of year, Earth ploughs straight through a comet's trail of dust. Then dozens of meteors an hour can streak across the sky. This is a meteor shower.

The Perseids peak around 12 August each year. They come from the dust of Comet Swift-Tuttle. The Geminids peak around 13 to 14 December and are often the richest shower of the year. Unusually, they come from an asteroid called Phaethon rather than a [[comet|comet]].

All the meteors in a shower seem to fly out from one point in the sky, like the view through a car windscreen as snow rushes towards you. Each shower is named after the [[constellation|constellation]] where that point lies.

Sometimes a shower becomes a storm. In November 1833, people across North America saw the Leonids fall so thickly that some thought the stars were dropping out of the sky. It became one of the most famous sky events in American history.

{{story:fire-burns}}

A bigger piece, perhaps the size of a marble or a football, makes a much brighter streak called a fireball. Very rarely, part of a space rock survives the fall and lands on the ground. That rock is called a [[@meteorites|meteorite]].

Scientists treasure [[meteorite|meteorites]]. Many are about 4.6 billion years old, left over from when the planets were forming. A few have even come from Mars and the Moon, knocked off by impacts long ago.

In 2013, a rock about 20 m wide exploded high above Chelyabinsk in Russia, brighter than the Sun for a moment. Rocks that big are rare. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] keep watch for them, as you can read in [[@asteroid-today|could an asteroid hit Earth today?]]

Lonar Lake in Maharashtra sits inside a bowl almost 2 km wide, blasted out when a large meteorite hit the Deccan's volcanic rock long ago. Scientists still debate exactly when that happened. The lake's water is salty and alkaline, and it sometimes turns pink, thanks to tiny living things in the water.

You don't need a telescope. Telescopes see only a small patch of sky, but meteors can appear anywhere. The best plan is to get far from city lights, lie back and look up. Meteor counts are often higher after midnight, when your side of Earth faces forward into the dust, like a car's windscreen in the rain.

text: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh roughly a billion tonnes, and possibly several times that. That is heavier than every one of the 8 billion people on Earth put together. It would also weigh more than ten thousand of the largest aircraft carriers.

Neutron stars are the crushed leftover cores of giant stars that blew up. They pack more mass than our Sun into a ball about 20 km across, about the size of a city, or roughly the length of Manhattan in New York. The matter inside is squeezed so tightly that the empty space inside [[atom|atoms]] has been crushed out.

st.reveal: A neutron star's gravity is so strong that even a 1-metre drop speeds things up to around 2,000 km every second. The marshmallow would hit with the energy of a few tonnes of explosive.

sec.h: Crushing the emptiness out of atoms
sec.t:
An atom is mostly empty. If the [[nucleus|nucleus]] at the centre were a cricket ball in the middle of a stadium, the [[electron|electrons]] would be like specks of dust in the outer stands. Everything in between is nothing.

Inside a neutron star, [[gravity|gravity]] is so strong that it crushes electrons into the nucleus. They combine with [[proton|protons]] to make neutrons. The neutrons then pack together almost touching, with all the emptiness gone. Squeeze the whole Earth that way and it would shrink to the size of a large football stadium.

In 1967, a research student at Cambridge named Jocelyn Bell Burnell noticed a strange signal in her radio telescope data. It pulsed exactly every 1.3 seconds. The team half-jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for "little green men". It turned out to be a spinning neutron star sweeping a beam of radio waves past Earth like a lighthouse. These stars are now called pulsars.

Some spin unbelievably fast. One pulsar turns 716 times a second. A ceiling fan on full speed manages about five. Neutron stars also carry the strongest magnets known. The most powerful kind, called magnetars, have magnetic fields so strong that from halfway to the Moon they could wipe the strip on a bank card. Closer in, they would pull apart the atoms in your body.

On the surface of a neutron star, gravity is around 200 billion times stronger than on Earth. A mountain could not rise more than a few millimetres before collapsing under its own weight. The surface is the smoothest of any known object.

If you dropped something from just 1 metre up, it would hit the ground at about 2,000 km per second. To launch a rocket off a neutron star, you would need to reach roughly a third of the speed of light.

Say you somehow scooped out a teaspoon and brought it to Earth. It wouldn't stay a teaspoon. Without the star's [[@gravity-planets|gravity]] holding it together, the neutrons would burst apart in a huge explosion of energy.

If it could stay squeezed, it would fall straight through your table, your floor and the ground. It would sink through the crust toward the centre of the Earth like a stone through water. Push gravity just a little further than a neutron star and you get something even stranger, an object so dense that not even light can climb back out.

text: Most small drones are quadcopters, with four [[propeller|propellers]] pointing up. Each one pushes air down, and the air pushes the drone up. By making some propellers spin faster than others, the drone can tilt, turn and move in any direction.

Flying "by itself" is the job of a small computer called the flight controller. It reads tiny motion [[sensor|sensors]] hundreds of times a second and adjusts each motor to keep the drone level. Add GPS and [[@cameras-how|cameras]], and a drone can hold its position in a breeze, follow a planned route, avoid obstacles and come home when its battery runs low.

st.prompt: A quadcopter wants to fly forward. What does its computer do?

options.t: Speeds up the back propellers so the drone tilts forward
Switches on a fifth propeller at the back
Stops all the propellers for a second

st.reveal: Spinning the back propellers a little faster lifts the back, so the drone tips nose-down. Now its propellers push air down and slightly backwards, and the drone moves forward. All its moves come from changing propeller speeds.

d.try: Balance a ruler or a long stick upright on the palm of your hand. Notice how your hand keeps making tiny, quick moves to stop it falling. A drone's computer does the same thing, but hundreds of times a second, by changing the speed of its propellers.

sec.t:
A quadcopter has no rudder or flaps. Everything comes from propeller speed.

Two propellers spin clockwise, and the two on the opposite corners spin anticlockwise. That way, their twisting forces cancel out, and the drone doesn't spin like a top. To rise, all four speed up. To move forward, the back two spin a bit faster, tipping the drone nose-down. To turn on the spot, the clockwise pair speeds up while the other pair slows, and the body twists round. It is the same problem a [[@helicopters|helicopter's]] tail [[rotor|rotor]] solves, done a different way.

More advanced drones use cameras and other sensors to "see" around them, like [[@self-driving|self-driving cars]]. They can spot a tree or a wall and steer around it. Some can follow a running person or a cyclist, keeping them in the camera frame.

Many drones can fly a mission set in advance. Someone taps points on a map, and the drone flies from one to the next, takes photos and lands. But a person usually still watches and can take control if something goes wrong.

Drones film cricket matches, weddings and wildlife. They inspect bridges, power lines and [[@wind-turbines|wind turbines]] without anyone having to climb. In Rwanda, a company called Zipline has used drones since 2016 to fly blood supplies to hospitals in hilly areas.

In India, drones spray crops on farms and map land. In 2023, the government launched a scheme to give drones to women's self-help groups, so they can offer spraying services to farmers. In January 2022, about 1,000 drones made glowing pictures over Delhi during the Beating Retreat ceremony, all flown by computers.

In the 1930s, Britain built a radio-controlled target plane called the Queen Bee, for gunners to practise on. Pilotless target planes soon became known as drones, the name for male bees. Many people say the buzzing sound of modern drones makes the name fit even better. Real [[@bees-dance|bees]], though, still beat drones at landing on a flower in a breeze.

Drones share the sky with planes, helicopters and birds, so there are rules. In India, the Drone Rules of 2021 divide the map into green, yellow and red zones. Red zones, such as areas around [[@airports|airports]], are off-limits without special permission. In the USA, the Federal Aviation Administration says most drones heavier than 250 g must be registered. Always fly with an adult, in an open space, away from people.

text: The pistol shrimp has one giant claw, sometimes half the size of its body. When it snaps the claw shut, a plunger on one half rams into a socket on the other and squirts out a jet of water at around 100 km/h. That is faster than a car on a highway, from a creature smaller than a crayon.

The jet moves so fast that the water pressure behind it drops and a bubble opens up, a process called cavitation. A split second later, the bubble collapses. For a tiny instant, the gas inside is squeezed so hard that it heats to an estimated 4,000 °C or more and gives off a flash of light. The Sun's surface is about 5,500 °C.

st.prompt: What actually stuns the pistol shrimp's prey?

options.t: The shock wave from a collapsing bubble
The two halves of the claw hitting the fish
Poison squirted from the claw

st.reveal: The claw never touches the prey. It shoots out a jet of water so fast that a bubble forms and then collapses with a bang. The shock wave stuns small fish and shrimp.

Smithsonian Ocean, snapping shrimp.
n.certNote: The snap, the bubble and the flash of light are well measured. The bubble's exact temperature is an estimate from the colour of the light, so figures vary from about 4,000 °C to 5,000 °C.

sec.t:
For years, people thought the snap was the sound of the claw clicking shut. In 2000, a team in the Netherlands filmed the snap with high-speed cameras and found the truth. The bang comes from the bubble collapsing, not from the claw.

The collapse sends out a shock wave strong enough to stun or kill small fish, worms and other shrimp nearby. The shrimp then drags its dinner into its burrow. It is a hunter with a gun made of water.

Close up, the snap is one of the loudest sounds made by any animal in the sea, about as loud as a gunshot at close range. Scientists who measure [[@extreme-loudest-animals|animal noises]] put it up there with whales.

There are hundreds of kinds of snapping shrimp living in warm, shallow seas, including around India's coasts and reefs. A healthy reef can have thousands of them, all snapping. Divers say it sounds like bacon frying or twigs crackling on a fire.

During the Second World War, American and British navies discovered this noise the hard way. Their underwater microphones picked up so much crackle that it hid other sounds. Submarines sometimes used shrimp beds as cover, because enemy listeners couldn't pick out their engines over the shrimp. Navies still study the noise for modern [[@submarines|submarines]].

Some pistol shrimp share their burrows with small fish called gobies. The shrimp is nearly blind, so it keeps one feeler touching the goby. When danger comes, the goby flicks its tail and both dive inside. The shrimp digs and cleans the burrow, and the goby keeps watch.

If a pistol shrimp loses its big claw, its small claw slowly grows into a new snapper, and a new small claw grows where the big one was. In other words, the shrimp switches hands. Its cousin, the [[@power-mantis-shrimp|mantis shrimp]], uses an even stranger weapon: a punch so fast it also boils the water.

text: Concrete is a mix of four simple things: cement, water, sand and gravel or crushed stone. Cement is a fine grey powder. When it meets water, it reacts and forms tiny crystals that grow and tangle together. Those crystals glue the sand and stones into an artificial rock.

The stones and sand make up most of the volume, and they give concrete its strength. The cement is the glue. Freshly mixed, concrete can be poured into any shape, like a thick grey batter. Within hours it stiffens. Within weeks it is strong enough to hold up a flyover. People pour so much of it that it is the most used building material on Earth.

Concrete keeps getting stronger for a long time. Builders usually test samples after 28 days, when they have reached most of their strength, but the reaction carries on slowly for years. That's why fresh concrete is kept damp, often under wet sacks, while it cures.

st.prompt: Builders sometimes pour fresh concrete into water, for bridge pillars and dock walls. What happens?

It washes away and never sets
It hardens only after the water is pumped out

st.reveal: Cement reacts with water to grow tiny crystals that lock the sand and stones together. It doesn't need air or sunshine, so with care it can set even underwater.

sec.t:
Cement starts as rock. Limestone, often formed from the shells of ancient sea creatures, is crushed and mixed with clay. The mix is heated in a huge rotating [[kiln|kiln]], a long tilted tube, to about 1,450 °C. The heat changes the rock into hard grey lumps called clinker.

The clinker is ground into powder with a little gypsum, a soft mineral that slows the setting so builders have time to work. The result is Portland cement, patented in England in 1824 and named after a pale building stone from the Isle of Portland. India is now the world's second-largest cement maker, after China. Many of its plants sit close to limestone deposits, in states such as Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

Concrete is very good at being squashed but bad at being stretched or bent. A concrete beam with nothing inside can crack in the middle under a heavy load.

The fix, worked out in the 1800s, was to bury [[@steel|steel]] rods inside. Steel is good at being stretched. Together they make reinforced concrete, which can span wide gaps and hold up tall buildings. Most bridges, metro stations, dams and [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] today rely on it. If water seeps in and the steel rusts, it swells and cracks the concrete from the inside, which is why old buildings sometimes shed chunks.

Making cement releases a lot of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. The fuel for the kiln gives some off. Heating limestone releases even more, because limestone is partly made of carbon dioxide locked in rock. Altogether, cement causes about 8% of the world's emissions, which feeds [[@climate-change|climate change]].

Scientists are working on fixes. Some mixes swap part of the cement for fly ash from power stations or slag from steel works. Others capture the carbon dioxide before it escapes, or press it back into fresh concrete. Since the world will keep building homes, roads and schools, a greener grey could matter a great deal.

text: Fire is what we see when something burns. Scientists call it [[combustion|combustion]]. It's a chemical reaction in which a fuel, such as wood, gas, wax or paper, joins with oxygen from the air. The reaction releases a lot of energy as heat and light, very quickly.

For a fire to start and keep going, it needs three things: fuel to burn, oxygen to join with it, and enough heat to get the reaction going. [[@jobs-firefighter|Firefighters]] call this the fire triangle. Take away any one side, and the fire goes out.
Once a fire starts, it makes its own heat. That heat warms nearby fuel, which starts to burn too. That's why a small flame can grow so quickly, and why fires need to be treated with great care.

st.prompt: When a log burns in a campfire, what is actually on fire?

The solid wood itself
The air around the log

st.reveal: Heat makes wood break down and release flammable gases. Those gases mix with oxygen in the air and burn, making the flames you see dancing above the log. The glowing embers left at the end are charcoal burning more slowly on its surface.

sec.t:
When wood or wax gets hot, it doesn't burn as a solid. It first breaks down and gives off gases. Those gases mix with oxygen and burn, and that glowing region is the flame.

Most [[@candles|candle]] and wood flames are yellow-orange because they contain tiny specks of soot, bits of unburned carbon. The specks get so hot that they glow, like the filament in an old [[@light-bulb|light bulb]]. A [[@cooking-gas|gas stove]] flame is usually blue, because the gas is mixed well with air before it burns. It burns more completely, with very little soot, and the blue comes from the reacting gas itself.

Flames point upwards because the hot gases are lighter than the cooler air around them. They rise, pulling fresh air in from below.

Fire changed human history. It gave people warmth, light, protection from animals and a way to cook food. Cooking makes many foods softer and safer to eat and gives the body more energy from them.

When people first learned to control fire is hard to pin down. In Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, scientists found burnt bones and plant ash about a million years old, which may be some of the earliest evidence. Other researchers think regular, everyday use of fire came much later, perhaps a few hundred thousand years ago.

The energy in a burning log came from the Sun. While the tree was growing, its leaves used sunlight to build sugars from water and [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], a process called [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Burning releases that stored energy again, and gives the carbon dioxide back to the air.

Burning and [[@rust|rusting]] are close relatives. Both happen when a substance joins with oxygen. Rusting is just very slow, and you can't feel the warmth it gives off. Fire is the same kind of reaction, sped up so much that it glows. [[@cars-engine|Car engines]], gas stoves and power stations all use burning, carefully controlled, to make heat and movement.

text: When a ship sits in water, it pushes some water out of the way. The water pushes back. That upward push is called [[buoyancy|buoyancy]], and it equals the weight of the water the ship has pushed aside. If the ship can push aside its own weight in water before it sinks too deep, it floats.

A solid lump of steel is about eight times heavier than the same amount of water, so it sinks straight away. A ship, though, is not a solid lump. Its steel is spread out into a huge, thin-walled bowl full of air. That bowl pushes aside a lot of water while weighing much less than that water would. Add up the steel, the air, the cargo and the crew, and the whole ship is lighter, for its size, than the sea. Engineers would say its average [[density|density]] is lower than water's.

st.prompt: You squash a sheet of aluminium foil into a tight ball and drop it in water. Then you fold another sheet into a little boat. What happens?

options.t: Both float, because foil is light
The ball sinks or sits low, and the boat floats high

st.reveal: The boat shape pushes aside much more water than the tight ball, so the water pushes back up on it much harder. Ships work the same way. A big hollow hull holds a lot of air and displaces a lot of water.

sec.t:
The largest container ships today are about 400 metres long, about as long as four American football fields laid end to end, or nearly 20 cricket pitches. They have room for over 20,000 standard 6-metre steel containers. In March 2021, one of them, the *Ever Given*, got stuck sideways in [[@suez-canal|the Suez Canal]] in Egypt and blocked one of the world's busiest shipping routes for six days.

In 2022, India commissioned INS *Vikrant*, its first aircraft carrier designed and built in the country, at Cochin Shipyard in [[@kerala|Kerala]]. It is 262 metres long and carries fighter jets on its deck, yet it floats as steadily as a much smaller boat.

Too much cargo and a ship sits dangerously low, where waves can wash over it. In the 1800s, many overloaded British ships sank with their crews. A member of [[parliament|parliament]] named Samuel Plimsoll campaigned for years until a law in 1876 required a mark painted on every British ship's side. Today load lines, often called Plimsoll lines, show the deepest a ship may safely sit, with separate marks for fresh water, [[@why-sea-salty|salty sea]], summer and winter.

Ships are also split inside into watertight compartments, so one hole doesn't flood the whole hull. When the [[@titanic|Titanic]] hit an iceberg in 1912, too many of its compartments were opened to the sea at once, and it sank.

A [[@submarines|submarine]] uses the same rule in both directions. To dive, it lets seawater into special tanks, so it becomes heavier for its size and sinks. To rise, it blows the water out with compressed air, becomes lighter, and floats back up.

Ice floats for a related reason. When water freezes, it expands, becoming a little less dense than liquid water. That's why [[@why-ice-floats|icebergs float]] with only about a tenth of their bulk above the waves, and why ships have long kept a careful lookout for them.

text: Under the smooth glass top of an induction stove sits a flat coil of copper wire. When you switch it on, electricity flows through the coil, changing direction tens of thousands of times a second. That creates a magnetic field above the stove that flips back and forth just as fast.

When you put an iron or steel pan on top, the flipping field makes electric currents swirl around inside the base of the pan. The metal resists these currents, and that resistance turns into heat, right in the pan. The glass only gets warm because the hot pan sits on it.
No flame, no glowing coil. The pan is the heater.

st.prompt: You put a steel pan and an aluminium pan of water side by side on two induction zones. What happens?

options.t: Both heat up equally
Only the steel pan gets hot
Only the aluminium pan gets hot

st.reveal: Most induction stoves need a pan made of iron or a magnetic kind of steel. The changing magnetic field grips it and makes strong currents that heat it. Aluminium and glass don't respond in the same way, so they stay cool unless they have a special steel layer on the bottom.

The magnetic field is weak and fades within a few centimetres of the stove top. Health agencies treat normal home use as safe. People with heart pacemakers are usually told to check with their doctor and keep a little distance.

sec.t:
The idea goes back to 1831, when the English scientist Michael Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field can make electricity flow in a nearby wire. This is called electromagnetic induction. It is how power stations [[@electricity-made|make electricity]]: spinning magnets near coils of wire push currents into the grid.

An induction stove runs that trick in reverse and in miniature. The coil makes a changing magnetic field, and the field makes currents inside the pan. Engineers call these swirling currents eddy currents, after the little whirlpools you see in a stream. Faraday himself never saw an induction stove. Electric cooking of this kind only reached homes in the second half of the 1900s, and became cheap enough for most families much later.

A gas flame heats the air around the pan as well as the pan itself. A lot of the heat escapes up the sides and into the kitchen. The US Department of Energy estimates that only about a third to two-fifths of a gas flame's energy reaches the food.

Induction is far better at this, at roughly 85 per cent, because the heat starts in the pan. Water can boil faster than on gas, and the kitchen stays cooler. Turning the dial changes the heat instantly, much like gas, which cooks appreciate.

Burning gas, wood or kerosene inside a home releases smoke and gases. In many Indian villages, cooking over wood or dung fires has been a major cause of indoor [[@air-pollution|air pollution]], which harms the lungs. Gas is much cleaner than wood, and induction adds no fumes at all. In the USA, some cities have started asking new buildings to use electric cooking instead of gas, partly for cleaner air and partly to cut the gases that warm the planet.

Induction has downsides. It needs electricity, which isn't always reliable, and the right pans, which cost money. The stove top stays hot for a while after cooking, from the pan's heat, so it still needs care. But a stove that heats only the pan is one of the quietest bits of physics in the house.

text: Music on your phone is stored as numbers. The phone turns those numbers into an electric signal that rises and falls very quickly, in the same pattern as the sound waves of the song.

That signal flows into a small coil of wire inside each earcup. The coil sits next to a [[@magnets-how|magnet]]. When current flows one way, the coil is pushed. When it flows the other way, the coil is pulled. The coil is glued to a thin, light disc called a [[diaphragm|diaphragm]], so the disc shakes in and out too.
The shaking disc pushes on the air in your ear, and that is [[@sound-travel|sound]].

sec.t:
To play a high note, the diaphragm moves back and forth thousands of times every second. To play a deep bass note, it moves fewer times, but further. A song is many notes at once, so the disc does all these wobbles together, in one complicated dance.

A loudspeaker on a stage works the same way. It just has a much bigger cone and a stronger magnet, because it has to shake a whole hall of air instead of the little space inside your ear.

In 1877, Thomas Edison's team in New Jersey built the phonograph. A needle cut wobbly grooves into a sheet of tinfoil wrapped round a turning cylinder. Run the needle along the groove again, and it played the sound back. One of the first things Edison recorded was the nursery rhyme "Mary had a little lamb".

Twenty years earlier, in 1857, a Frenchman named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville built a machine that drew sound waves as squiggly lines on paper blackened with soot. He never meant them to be played. In 2008, researchers in the USA used computers to turn one of his squiggles from 1860 back into sound. They heard a few seconds of a voice singing the French song "Au clair de la lune".

India's music was recorded early too. In 1902, the singer Gauhar Jaan recorded songs in Calcutta for the Gramophone Company. She became one of the first Indian performers whose voice could be bought and played at home.

Early headphones were heavy and meant for [[@telephone|telephone]] operators. In 1910, an inventor named Nathaniel Baldwin built a better pair at his kitchen table in Utah. The US Navy wanted them for radio operators, and soon he was making them in large numbers. [[@radio-invented|Radio]] helped headphones become common in homes.

Today, sound is stored as numbers. A CD measures the sound wave 44,100 times every second and writes down each measurement. A phone keeps songs in files that squeeze those numbers to save space, as described in [[@data-storage|data storage]].

Noise-cancelling headphones add another trick. [[@microphones|Small microphones]] on the outside listen to the hum of a bus or an aeroplane. The headphones then play the exact opposite wave, and the two cancel out, leaving much less noise. The quietest sound in your headphones can be one the speaker is making on purpose.

text: मध्य प्रदेश में भीमबेटका के [[prehistoric|शैलाश्रयों]] में भारत के सबसे पुराने ज्ञात चित्रों में से कुछ हैं। इनमें बाइसन, हिरण, बाघ, हाथी, गैंडे और जंगली सूअर जैसे जानवर हैं। लोग धनुष और भालों से शिकार करते, कतार में नाचते, घोड़ों और हाथियों पर सवारी करते, शहद इकट्ठा करते और ढोल बजाते दिखते हैं।

ये चित्र बहुत लंबे समय में बने। माना जाता है कि सबसे पुराने चित्र पाषाण युग के आखिरी दौर के हैं, शायद 10,000 साल से भी ज़्यादा पुराने। कुछ कहीं नए हैं, शुरुआती राजाओं के ज़माने के, जिनमें घुड़सवार और सिपाही हैं। सब मिलाकर ये हज़ारों सालों में फैली मध्य भारत की इंसानी ज़िंदगी की एक तस्वीरों वाली किताब जैसे हैं।

sec.h: ट्रेन की खिड़की से हुई खोज
sec.t:
भीमबेटका विंध्य की पहाड़ियों में, भोपाल से लगभग 45 किलोमीटर दक्षिण में है। आसपास के लोग इन चट्टानों को अच्छी तरह जानते थे। पर 1957 में [[archaeologist|पुरातत्वविद्]] विष्णु श्रीधर वाकणकर ट्रेन से जा रहे थे, तभी उनकी नज़र पहाड़ियों पर अजीब-सी चट्टानों पर पड़ी। उन्हें स्पेन और फ़्रांस की चित्रों वाली गुफाएँ याद आ गईं।

वे खोजबीन के लिए लौटे और उन्हें एक के बाद एक चित्रों से भरे शैलाश्रय मिलते गए। अगले कुछ सालों में उन्होंने और दूसरे शोधकर्ताओं ने इस इलाके में लगभग 700 शैलाश्रय दर्ज किए। 2003 में यूनेस्को ने भीमबेटका को विश्व धरोहर स्थल बनाया। इस नाम को अक्सर [[@mahabharata|महाभारत]] के नायक भीम से जोड़ा जाता है, और इसका मतलब कुछ-कुछ "भीम के बैठने की जगह" है।

कुछ सबसे पुराने चित्रों में गैंडे और बाइसन जैसे बड़े जानवर मोटी लकीरों से, असल से भी बड़े बनाए गए हैं। एक मशहूर चट्टान, जिसे ज़ू रॉक यानी चिड़ियाघर वाली चट्टान कहते हैं, हाथियों, हिरणों, बाइसनों और दूसरे जानवरों से भरी है, जिन्हें अलग-अलग समय में अलग-अलग लोगों ने बनाया।

गैंडों के चित्र हैरान करते हैं। आज भारत के एक सींग वाले गैंडे मुख्य रूप से दूर पूर्वोत्तर में, असम में रहते हैं, जैसे [[@rhino-kaziranga|काज़ीरंगा]] में। चित्र बताते हैं कि कभी गैंडे मध्य भारत में भी रहते थे।

शिकार के दृश्यों में लोग धनुष-बाण, भाले और फंदे लिए दिखते हैं। कुछ जानवरों के शरीर के अंदर लकीरों या बिंदियों के नमूने बने हैं, मानो उनका एक्स-रे लिया गया हो।

{{story:cave-art}}

भीमबेटका के लोग सिर्फ़ शिकार ही नहीं बनाते थे। आकृतियों की कतारें हाथ पकड़कर नाचती हैं। कुछ ढोल बजाती हैं। कुछ चित्रों में लोग छत्तों से शहद उतारते दिखते हैं, जो भारत के जंगलों में आज भी होता है। माँएँ बच्चों को उठाए हैं, और टोलियाँ किसी चीज़ के चारों ओर जुटी हैं, जो शायद आग हो।

नए चित्रों में लोग घोड़ों और हाथियों पर सवार हैं और तलवारें और ढालें लिए हैं। ये बाद के दौर के हैं, जब राज्य और सेनाएँ आ चुकी थीं। दीवारें दिखाती हैं कि ज़िंदगी शिकार और कंद-मूल बटोरने से खेती और लड़ाइयों की ओर कैसे बदली।

चित्रकारों ने मुख्य रूप से लाल और सफ़ेद रंग लगाए, थोड़ा पीला और हरा भी। लाल रंग [[ochre|गेरू]] और हेमेटाइट से आया, जो लोहे से भरपूर पत्थर हैं और जिन्हें पीसकर चूरा बनाया जाता था। सफ़ेद रंग चूना पत्थर या खड़िया जैसी मिट्टी से आया। शायद वे इन्हें पानी, पेड़ के गोंद या चर्बी में मिलाते थे।

ब्रश शायद टहनियों या पौधों के रेशों से बने होते थे, जिनका सिरा चबाकर नरम किया जाता। कुछ चित्र उँगलियों से बने। शैलाश्रय बारिश से बचे रहते हैं, इसलिए बहुत-से चित्र हज़ारों साल से टिके हैं, हालाँकि कुछ फीके पड़ गए हैं।

भीमबेटका में चित्रों से बहुत पहले भी इंसानों के रहने के निशान मिलते हैं। यहाँ मिले पत्थर के औज़ार बताते हैं कि इंसान और उनके [[ancestor|पूर्वज]] इन शैलाश्रयों में बहुत लंबे समय तक, शायद लाखों साल तक रहे। कुछ शोधकर्ता मानते हैं कि यहाँ चट्टान में खुदे छोटे कटोरी जैसे गड्ढे दुनिया में इंसान के बनाए सबसे पुराने निशानों में से हैं।

फ़्रांस की लास्को की चित्रों वाली गुफाओं की तरह भीमबेटका भी दिखाता है कि इंसान हमेशा से तस्वीरें बनाना चाहता रहा है। भीमबेटका के पहले चित्रकारों के हज़ारों साल बाद पश्चिमी भारत के कलाकारों ने [[@ajanta-colours|अजंता]] की बौद्ध गुफाओं को कहीं ज़्यादा भरपूर रंगों से भर दिया। उन्होंने यह कैसे किया, वह अपने आप में एक अलग कहानी है।

sec.t:
पारंपरिक लकड़ी है *आले मर*, जिसे कभी-कभी आइवरी वुड भी कहते हैं, क्योंकि यह हल्के रंग की और महीन रेशों वाली होती है। यह इतनी नरम है कि आसानी से तराशी जा सके, पर आकार अच्छी तरह पकड़े रखती है। कारीगर लट्ठों को गुटकों में काटकर काम शुरू करने से पहले सूखने के लिए छोड़ देते हैं।

गुटके को खराद पर कस दिया जाता है, जो उसे बहुत तेज़ी से घुमाती है। कारीगर उस पर छेनी टिकाता है और लकड़ी के छल्ले छीलता जाता है, कुछ-कुछ वैसे जैसे पेंसिल का शार्पनर, बस बाहर से काम करता हुआ। कुछ ही मिनटों में खुरदरा गुटका एकदम गोल गेंद, शंकु या छल्ला बन जाता है। पुरानी खरादें हाथ या पैर से चलती थीं। आज ज़्यादातर बिजली से चलती हैं।

क्योंकि सब कुछ गोल-गोल घुमाकर बनता है, इसलिए चन्नपटना के खिलौने गोल आकारों से भरे होते हैं: गेंदें, चकतियाँ, छल्ले और शंकु। हुनरमंद कारीगर इन्हें जोड़कर पेचीदा खिलौने बना लेते हैं। एक के ऊपर एक चढ़ने वाले छल्लों का सेट बस खराद पर बनी कुछ चकतियाँ हैं, जो खराद पर बने एक डंडे में पिरोई गई हैं। एक छोटी खिलौना कार में खराद पर बना एक ढाँचा और खराद पर बने चार पहिए हो सकते हैं।

चन्नपटना में बहुत-से लोग कहते हैं कि यह कला टीपू सुल्तान के समय से चली आ रही है, जो 1700 के दशक के आख़िर में [[@mysore-palace|मैसूर]] के [[monarch|शासक]] थे। इस किस्से के मुताबिक उन्होंने स्थानीय कारीगरों को सिखाने के लिए फ़ारस से लकड़ी के कारीगर बुलवाए। किस्सा मशहूर है, पर इसकी पुष्टि करने वाले लिखित सबूत बहुत कम हैं।

ज़्यादा पक्की जानकारी बाद की है। 20वीं सदी की शुरुआत में बावस मियाँ नाम के एक स्थानीय कारीगर को नई [[technology|तकनीकें]] लाने और बहुत-से परिवारों को यह काम सिखाने का श्रेय दिया जाता है। अगले दशकों में यह शहर अपने लाख वाले खिलौनों के लिए पूरे भारत में मशहूर हो गया। परिवारों ने यह हुनर माता-पिता से बच्चों तक पहुँचाया, और पूरी-पूरी गलियाँ छोटी-छोटी कार्यशालाओं से भर गईं, जहाँ खरादों की घरघराहट गूँजती और फ़र्श पर लकड़ी के छिलकों के ढेर लगे रहते।

1990 और 2000 के दशक तक सस्ते [[@plastic-made|प्लास्टिक]] खिलौनों से बाज़ार पट गए, और चन्नपटना की बहुत-सी कार्यशालाएँ मुश्किल में पड़ गईं। कुछ कारीगर दूसरे काम-धंधों में चले गए।

तब डिज़ाइनर, दस्तकारी से जुड़े संगठन और सरकार आगे आए। उन्होंने कारीगरों को पहेलियाँ, गहने और पढ़ाई में काम आने वाले आधुनिक खिलौने जैसे नए डिज़ाइन बनाने में मदद की, और उन्हें ऑनलाइन और विदेश की दुकानों को बेचना सिखाया। चन्नपटना के खिलौनों और गुड़ियों को जीआई टैग भी मिला, जो यह नाम इस इलाके में बने खिलौनों के लिए सुरक्षित रखता है। आज [[@karnataka|कर्नाटक]] से बहुत दूर की खिलौनों की दुकानों में भी चन्नपटना के [[@yo-yo-tops|लट्टू]] मिल जाते हैं, जो पहले की तरह ही धीरे-धीरे, धीरज से बनाए जाते हैं।

text: रेम्ब्रांट वान राइन नीदरलैंड्स के चित्रकार और छापाकार थे, जो 1606 से 1669 तक जिए। उन्हें अक्सर अब तक के सबसे महान कलाकारों में गिना जाता है। उन्होंने व्यक्ति-चित्र, बाइबल की कहानियाँ और बड़े-बड़े समूह दृश्य बनाए, और एचिंग नाम के सुंदर छापे भी तैयार किए।

उनकी ख़ासियत थी रोशनी का इस्तेमाल। उनकी तस्वीरों में लगता है जैसे रोशनी की एक किरण किसी एक चेहरे या एक हाथ पर पड़ रही हो और बाकी सब गर्म परछाईं में डूबा हो। उन्होंने लगभग 80 बार अपना ही चित्र बनाया, एक अकड़ू नौजवान से लेकर झुर्रियों वाले बूढ़े तक। उन आत्मचित्रों को क्रम से देखना ऐसा है जैसे किसी की पूरी ज़िंदगी की डायरी के पन्ने पलटना।

sec.t:
रेम्ब्रांट का जन्म विश्वविद्यालय वाले शहर लाइडन में एक चक्कीवाले के घर हुआ। उन्हें विश्वविद्यालय भेजा गया, पर जल्दी ही वे पढ़ाई छोड़कर चित्रकारी सीखने लगे। 1630 के दशक की शुरुआत में वे [[@amsterdam|एम्स्टर्डम]] आ गए, जो तब धरती के सबसे अमीर शहरों में था और व्यापार से मालामाल हुए सौदागरों से भरा था।

ये सौदागर अपने चित्र बनवाना चाहते थे, और जल्दी ही रेम्ब्रांट की माँग बढ़ गई। 1634 में उन्होंने सास्किया वान उइलेनबर्ग से शादी की और एक बड़ा, महँगा मकान ख़रीदा। उन्होंने दुनिया भर से सीपियाँ, कवच, छापे और कलाकृतियाँ इकट्ठा कीं, जिन्हें वे अपनी पेंटिंग में सामान की तरह इस्तेमाल करते थे।

1642 में रेम्ब्रांट ने एम्स्टर्डम के नगर रक्षकों की एक टुकड़ी की विशाल पेंटिंग पूरी की। यह लगभग 3.6 मीटर ऊँची और 4 मीटर से ज़्यादा चौड़ी है, यानी किसी आम घर की एक मंज़िल से भी ऊँची। आदमियों को सीधी कतार में खड़ा करने के बजाय उन्होंने उन्हें हरकत में आते दिखाया, साथ में एक ढोल बजाने वाला, एक कुत्ता और रोशनी के घेरे में खड़ी सुनहरे कपड़ों वाली एक लड़की।

बाद में दीवार पर फ़िट करने के लिए तस्वीर को चारों तरफ़ से काट दिया गया। सालों में इसकी वार्निश इतनी काली पड़ गई कि लोग इसे *द नाइट वॉच* कहने लगे। आज यह एम्स्टर्डम के राइक्सम्यूज़ियम में टँगी है। 2019 से वहाँ के वैज्ञानिक और [[conservator|संरक्षक]] "ऑपरेशन नाइट वॉच" नाम की परियोजना में [[@x-rays|एक्स-रे]] और दूसरे औज़ारों से इसकी एक-एक परत जाँच रहे हैं।

1650 के दशक के आख़िर में रेम्ब्रांट ने [[@mughal-miniatures|मुग़ल लघुचित्रों]] पर आधारित लगभग दो दर्जन चित्र बनाए। मुग़ल लघुचित्र भारत के बादशाहों के लिए बनी छोटी पेंटिंग थीं। उन्होंने शाहजहाँ, जहाँगीर और दरबारी अमीरों की आकृतियों की नकल की, शायद उन पेंटिंग से जो डच व्यापारी पूरब से लाए थे। उन्होंने मुद्राएँ तो वैसी ही रखीं, पर अपनी खुली-खुली शैली में बनाईं।

कोई ठीक-ठीक नहीं जानता कि उन्होंने ये चित्र क्यों बनाए। शायद उन्हें बस बारीक काम और शानदार पोशाकें भा गई थीं। जो भी हो, इससे पता चलता है कि व्यापार ने एम्स्टर्डम के एक चित्रकार को हज़ारों किलोमीटर दूर [[@mughals|मुग़ल]] [[emperor|सम्राटों]] के दरबार से कैसे जोड़ दिया।

रेम्ब्रांट की ज़िंदगी में दुख बहुत थे। सास्किया की मौत 1642 में हुई, उसी साल जब *द नाइट वॉच* बनी। उनके चार में से तीन बच्चे बचपन में ही चल बसे। वे जितना कमाते, उससे ज़्यादा ख़र्च करते, और 1656 में दिवालिया हो गए। उनका घर और उनका संग्रह बिक गया।

फिर भी वे काम करते रहे। उनकी कुछ सबसे बढ़िया पेंटिंग उनके आख़िरी, सबसे ग़रीबी भरे सालों की हैं, जिनमें वे आत्मचित्र भी हैं जो बिना किसी चापलूसी के उनके चेहरे की हर लकीर दिखाते हैं। उनका पुराना घर अब रेम्ब्रांट हाउस म्यूज़ियम है, जहाँ लोग वह कमरा देख सकते हैं जहाँ वे कभी चित्र बनाते थे।

text: What happens after a disaster follows a rough order. First comes rescue, getting people out of danger and treating the injured. Then relief: food, clean water, shelter and medicine for survivors. After that comes recovery, which means rebuilding homes, roads, schools and livelihoods. That part can take years.

Before any of this, there is preparation. Good warnings, practice drills and strong buildings save more lives than any rescue. In India, disaster work is led by the National Disaster Management Authority and carried out by state teams and the National Disaster Response Force. In the US, the [[federal|federal]] agency FEMA supports states and towns.

st.prompt: After a big earthquake, who usually rescues the most people trapped in rubble?

options.t: Neighbours and local people, in the first few hours
International rescue teams who fly in
Army helicopters

st.reveal: Professional teams are skilled, but they often take hours or days to arrive. Many survivors are dug out early by the people living around them, which is why first-aid and safety training for ordinary people matters so much.

d.try: Make a family emergency card. Write down two phone numbers to call, a meeting place near home and one outside your area, and where the torch, water and first-aid kit are kept. Stick it on the fridge and check it with your family once a year.
myth: After a disaster, people usually panic and turn on each other.
Studies of disasters show the opposite is far more common. People tend to stay calm, help strangers, share food and organise themselves long before official help arrives.
facts: about 10 lakh people evacuated in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh

sec.t:
The first 72 hours matter most. Trapped people need air, water and medical help quickly. The very first rescuers are usually neighbours, shopkeepers, teachers and passers-by, who dig through rubble with their hands or wade into floodwater with ropes.

Then trained teams arrive. In India, the NDRF has battalions placed around the country so they can reach a disaster quickly. They bring cutting tools, boats, sniffer dogs, and cameras on poles that can look into gaps in the rubble. Fire services, police and the armed forces join in, using helicopters to reach cut-off villages.

In October 1999, a super [[cyclone|cyclone]] struck Odisha. Warnings did not reach many villages in time, and about 10,000 people died. Odisha then built hundreds of cyclone shelters, set up volunteer teams in villages and practised evacuations.

When Cyclone Phailin approached in October 2013, the India Meteorological Department tracked it days ahead using [[@weather-satellites|weather satellites]]. About 10 lakh people were moved to safety in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. A few dozen people died. The UN praised the effort, and Odisha's approach has been copied in other countries.

Recovery is the slowest stage. Houses must be rebuilt, often to stronger designs. Farmers need seeds and tools. Children need schools to reopen, because routine helps them cope. Governments, charities and insurance companies share the costs.

The aim is often to "build back better". After the 2001 earthquake in Gujarat, many rebuilt homes in Kutch followed rules to make them safer in future [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]]. After the 2004 Indian Ocean [[tsunami|tsunami]], India joined other countries in setting up a [[@tsunami-warning|tsunami warning]] centre, which opened in Hyderabad in 2007.

Children can help a great deal, mostly by being prepared. Learn your address and a parent's phone number by heart. Agree on where to meet if your family gets separated. Know the emergency number: 112 in India and 911 in the US. These are real safety skills, and many adults don't have them.

Many schools hold earthquake and fire drills. In an earthquake, the advice is to drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. Learning basic [[@first-aid|first aid]] is another way to be useful. After a disaster, relief groups usually say money helps more than old clothes, because it lets them buy exactly what is needed close to the disaster zone. A school fundraiser can reach a family who has lost almost everything.

text: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that can only be divided exactly by 1 and by itself. The first few are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13. A number like 12 is not prime, because it can be made by multiplying 3 × 4 or 2 × 6. Numbers like that are called composite.

Primes are the building blocks of all whole numbers. Every whole number above 1 can be made by multiplying primes together, in exactly one way. For example, 60 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Primes look simple, but they hold some of the [[@unsolved-problems|oldest unsolved puzzles]] in maths, and they keep your messages safe online.

st.prompt: In 1974, scientists beamed a message into space made of exactly 1,679 on-off signals. Why choose 1,679?

options.t: It can be split only one way, into 23 rows of 73, so aliens could arrange it as a picture
It was the year the telescope was first imagined
It is the number of stars in our galaxy

st.reveal: 1,679 is 23 times 73, and both are prime. That means the signals can only be laid out in a grid of 23 by 73, or 73 by 23. Laid out the right way, they form a simple picture of numbers, DNA, a human figure and the telescope that sent it.

n.certNote: The maths of prime numbers is certain. The idea that cicadas evolved prime-numbered life cycles to avoid predators is a popular theory that scientists still debate.

d.try: Draw a grid of the numbers 1 to 100. Cross out 1. Circle 2, then cross out every other multiple of 2. Circle 3 and cross out its multiples. Keep going with the next number that is not crossed out. The circled numbers left are the primes. This method is called the Sieve of Eratosthenes, after a Greek scholar who lived over 2,000 years ago.
myth: 1 is a prime number.

A prime must have exactly two different factors, 1 and itself. The number 1 has only one factor. Mathematicians also leave it out because otherwise every number could be split into primes in endless ways, like 6 = 2 × 3 × 1 × 1.
facts: a whole number above 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself
Proof that primes never run out

sec.t:
Think of primes like [[atom|atoms]] in chemistry. Just as water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, 30 is made of 2, 3 and 5. No matter how you start splitting a number, you always end with the same primes. This rule is so important that it is called the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

Two is the only even prime, because every other [[@even-odd|even number]] can be divided by 2. After that, primes become rarer as numbers get bigger, but they never stop. Around 300 BCE, the Greek mathematician [[@euclid|Euclid]] proved there are infinitely many. His proof is short and clever, and mathematicians still admire it.

Multiplying two primes is easy. Try 13 × 17, and you get 221. But going backwards is much harder. If someone gives you a huge number and says it is two primes multiplied, finding them could take the fastest computers longer than the age of the universe.

Many systems that keep data safe online use this idea. Your browser, banking apps and payment systems rely on maths built on primes and other hard problems. That is part of what protects your [[@passwords|passwords]] and card details as they travel across the [[@internet-how|internet]]. Learn how [[@cipher-codes|secret codes]] have changed over time.

In 1974, [[astronomer|astronomers]] used the giant Arecibo radio telescope in [[@puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] to beam a message towards a cluster of stars about 25,000 light years away. They chose a length of 1,679 signals because it is 23 × 73, the product of two primes. A clever listener would realise the signal can only be arranged as a grid of 23 by 73, and see a picture appear. Nobody expects a reply soon, but scientists hope primes would be a sign of intelligence anywhere, as you can read in [[@alien-life|alien life]].

In the eastern United States, some kinds of [[@maths-prime-cicadas|cicadas]] spend 13 or 17 years underground, then emerge in their billions at once. Both numbers are prime. One theory says prime cycles make it harder for [[predator|predators]] with shorter cycles to time their own numbers to match. [[biologist|Biologists]] still debate whether that is the real reason.

Some prime puzzles remain unsolved after centuries. In 1742 Christian Goldbach guessed that every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes, like 10 = 3 + 7. Computers have checked it for enormous numbers, but nobody has proved it is always true.

text: The Commonwealth Games are a big multi-sport event, a bit like a smaller [[@olympics|Olympics]]. They are held every four years. The athletes come from the nations of the Commonwealth, a group of mostly English-speaking countries that were once part of the British Empire.
There are swimmers and sprinters, boxers and weightlifters, cyclists and netball players. Para-athletes compete at the same Games, and their medals count in the same table.
India has taken part since 1934. It hosted the Games in Delhi in 2010, and Ahmedabad was chosen in November 2025 to host the 2030 Games, exactly a hundred years after the first.

st.reveal: Glasgow took over the 2026 Games at short notice and kept costs down by holding just 10 sports in four venues. Shooting, wrestling, badminton and hockey were all dropped, which hurt India's medal hopes. India still finished fourth.

myth: The Commonwealth Games are only for countries that Britain still rules.

Almost all the teams come from independent countries. The Commonwealth is a voluntary club of nations, most of which used to be part of the British Empire, and a few, such as Rwanda and Mozambique, were never British colonies at all. Only a handful of small teams, such as Gibraltar and Bermuda, still come from British territories.

sec.t:
The first Games were held in Hamilton, Canada, in 1930. They were called the British Empire Games, and about 400 athletes from 11 teams took part.

At that time Britain ruled a huge [[empire|empire]], including India. After the Second World War, country after country won its freedom, and [[@decolonisation|India became independent]] in 1947. Many of these new nations chose to stay linked in a friendly club, the Commonwealth.

The Games changed name to match. Since 1978 they have simply been the Commonwealth Games. Today about 70 teams take part, because places like Scotland, Wales, Jersey and the Isle of Man each enter their own.

People often call them "the friendly games". Athletes from tiny island nations share the track with world champions. Rugby sevens, netball and lawn bowls get a big stage here, though they are rare or absent at the Olympics.

Since 2002 the Games have mixed para-sport into the main programme, with events for athletes with disabilities held alongside the others. Birmingham 2022 also gave out more medals to women than to men, a first for any big multi-sport games.

Before each Games, a baton carrying a message from the head of the Commonwealth travels through the member nations, a bit like the [[@pop-olympic-torch|Olympic torch]]. The relay began in 1958 and now visits dozens of countries on its way to the host city.

{{story:paralympics}}

For India, the Games have long been a medal feast. Indian shooters, [[@wrestling-india|wrestlers]], weightlifters, boxers and badminton players often finish on the podium. At Delhi 2010 India won 101 medals, its best ever, and came second in the table behind Australia.

In 1958, in Cardiff, the sprinter [[@milkha-singh|Milkha Singh]] won the 440 yards race, giving independent India its first Commonwealth gold in athletics. Many Indian sporting heroes since have first become famous here. A Commonwealth medal often leads to an Olympic one a few years later.

The 2026 Games were meant to be held in Victoria, Australia, but the state pulled out in 2023 because of rising costs. Glasgow, which had hosted the Games in 2014, stepped in at short notice. To keep things cheap it held just 10 sports in four venues, from 23 July to 2 August 2026.

Many of India's best events, including shooting, wrestling, badminton, hockey and [[@table-tennis|table tennis]], were left out. Even so, India won 39 medals, 13 of them gold, and finished fourth.

Not everyone loves the Games. Some people say they are too expensive for host cities. Others feel uneasy that an event born from the British Empire still celebrates those old links.

Supporters answer that the Games give smaller nations a rare chance to shine, and that the Commonwealth today is a club of equals. Ahmedabad's centenary Games in 2030 will test which side is right. The city already has the [[@stadiums|Narendra Modi Stadium]], the largest cricket ground in the world.

text: Formula One is the top level of single-seater motor racing, using some of the most advanced [[@cars-engine|car engines]] ever built. Eleven teams each run two cars, and the 22 drivers race at about 24 Grands Prix a season on tracks around the world. Drivers earn points for finishing in the top ten: 25 for a win, 18 for second, and so on. The driver with the most points at the end of the season is world champion. There is also a title for the best team.
The "formula" is the set of rules every car must follow, from its weight to its engine size. Teams build their own cars within those rules, so engineering is as important as driving.

st.reveal: Cockpits get very hot, and drivers wear fireproof suits. In hot races such as Singapore, drivers can lose 2 to 3 kilograms of water. They drink through a tube in their helmets during the race.

d.try: Hold a sheet of paper just below your lips and blow over the top of it. The paper rises, because faster-moving air above it has lower pressure. Formula One wings use the same idea upside down, so the air pushes the car down instead of lifting it.
myth: Formula One is just about who has the fastest car.
The car matters a lot, but races are also won by tyre choices, pit stop timing, strategy in the rain and the driver's skill at overtaking. Teammates with the same car often finish far apart.

sec.h: Cars that stick to the road
sec.t:
A Formula One car can reach about 350 km/h on a long straight. Its secret is in the corners. The wings at the front and back work like aeroplane wings turned upside down. Instead of [[lift|lift]], they create [[downforce|downforce]], pushing the car onto the track.

At high speeds this force is greater than the weight of the car, which lets drivers take corners much faster than a normal car could. Engineers often say a Formula One car could, in theory, drive upside down on a ceiling at high enough speed, though nobody has tried.

[[@tyres|Tyres]] wear out during a race, and the rules make drivers use at least two different types of dry tyre. So at least once, drivers stop in the pit lane. About 20 crew members change all four wheels, often in around two seconds. The fastest stops have been under 2 seconds.

When to stop is a big strategy decision. Stopping early can help a driver jump ahead, but the new tyres must last to the end. Rain changes everything. Teams must guess when to switch to grooved wet tyres, and one good guess can win a race.

Safety has improved hugely. Since 2018 every car has had a halo, a curved titanium bar over the cockpit that protects the driver's head. Many drivers disliked its look at first, but it has since been credited with saving lives in crashes.

Drivers need strength as well as skill. In fast corners they feel forces up to about five times their body weight, and their necks must hold up a heavy helmet. In hot races they can lose 2 to 3 kilograms in sweat.

Michael Schumacher of Germany and Lewis Hamilton of Britain have each won seven world titles. Hamilton is the only Black driver to have raced in Formula One. The first Indian driver was Narain Karthikeyan from Coimbatore, who raced in 2005.

sec.h: Formula One in India and the USA
sec.t:
India hosted the Indian Grand Prix at the Buddh International Circuit near Greater Noida from 2011 to 2013. Sebastian Vettel won all three races. The race then stopped, partly over tax and cost disagreements.

In the USA, Formula One was once less popular than NASCAR. A Netflix series, *Drive to Survive*, brought in many new fans. By 2023 the USA had three races a year, in Austin, [[@miami|Miami]] and [[@las-vegas|Las Vegas]].

text: Ganesh Chaturthi is a Hindu festival that celebrates the birth of Ganesh, the elephant-headed god. Many Hindus pray to Ganesh before starting anything new, because he is believed to remove obstacles. The festival falls in the month of Bhadrapada, usually in late August or September.

Families bring home a clay image of Ganesh, decorate a small shrine and offer prayers, flowers and sweets. After a day and a half, five, seven or ten days, the image is carried to a river, lake or the sea for immersion. In Maharashtra, especially [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] and Pune, the festival fills the streets with music, drums and huge public idols.

st.prompt: Many Ganesh idols used to be made of plaster of Paris. Why do cities now ask people to choose clay instead?

options.t: Plaster does not dissolve easily and pollutes rivers and the sea
Clay idols are lighter to carry
Plaster cannot be painted

st.reveal: Plaster of Paris idols can take months to break down in water, and their paints may contain harmful chemicals. Natural clay idols dissolve quickly, so many families now choose them or immerse idols in a bucket or artificial pond.

sec.h: How Ganesh got his elephant head
sec.t:
There are several stories, but the best known goes like this. The goddess Parvati made a boy from clay and asked him to guard her door while she bathed. When her husband Shiva came home, the boy did not know him and refused to let him in.

In anger, Shiva cut off the boy's head. Parvati was heartbroken. To make amends, Shiva promised to bring the boy back to life and replaced his head with that of an elephant. He made Ganesh the leader of his followers and declared that people would worship Ganesh first, before any other god.

sec.h: Tilak takes it to the streets

sec.t:
Ganesh is said to love modaks, sweet dumplings filled with coconut and [[@jaggery|jaggery]]. In Maharashtra they are traditionally steamed in rice-flour shells shaped like little pouches. Families often offer 21 of them.

Every evening, families sing aartis, songs of prayer, with clapping and bells. Out on the streets, groups of drummers playing big dhol-tasha drums practise for weeks and lead the processions.

In Mumbai, some public idols are taller than a two-storey house. The most famous, the Lalbaugcha Raja in Lalbaug, has been set up by a local committee since 1934. Millions of people visit it during the festival, waiting in queues that can last many hours.

Ganesh also has an old link with writing. According to one legend, he wrote down the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] as the sage Vyasa recited it. That is why he is sometimes shown holding a broken tusk as a pen.

On Anant Chaturdashi, the last day, huge processions carry the idols to the sea at places like Girgaon Chowpatty in Mumbai. People chant "Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya", which means "Lord Ganpati, come back soon next year."

Immersion has caused problems. Idols made of plaster of Paris and painted with chemical colours do not [[dissolve|dissolve]] easily and harm fish and water. Many families now choose clay idols or immerse them at home in a bucket, then use the clay in the garden. Cities also build artificial ponds, so the water can be [[@water-purify|cleaned]] afterwards. Similar changes have reached [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]'s [[@durga-puja|Durga Puja]] too.

text: Mithali Raj is one of the greatest batters in the history of women's cricket. She played for India from 1999 to 2022, about 23 years, the longest international career of any woman cricketer. She scored 7,805 runs in one-day internationals, more than any other woman.

She captained India for many years and led them to two World Cup finals, in 2005 and 2017. Both were lost, but the 2017 run changed how Indians watched women's cricket. Millions tuned in, and a new generation of girls picked up bats.

It was the first century ever by an Indian woman
It was scored on the first day of her career

st.reveal: Her 214 at Taunton was the highest individual score in women's Test cricket at the time. Pakistan's Kiran Baloch passed it with 242 in 2004. Mithali was still a teenager.

India's women played their first Test in 1976 and their first one-day international in 1978. What changed recently is the attention, money and television coverage.

sec.h: From dance class to the nets
sec.t:
Mithali was born in Jodhpur, Rajasthan, in 1982, and grew up in Secunderabad, part of [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]]. As a little girl she learnt [[@bharatanatyam|Bharatanatyam]], the [[@indian-classical-dance|classical dance]] of Tamil Nadu, for several years.

Her father, an officer in the Indian Air Force, took her to cricket practice partly to cure her habit of sleeping late. Her brother was already training. Coaches noticed her neat, calm batting, and she soon had to choose between dance and cricket. She chose cricket, though she has said dance helped her footwork and balance at the crease.

In 2017 India reached the Women's World Cup final at Lord's in London. Before batting in some matches, Mithali was photographed calmly reading a book in the dressing room, and fans loved it. The final against England was tight, but India lost by nine runs.

It still felt like a turning point. Stadiums and television audiences grew. Players like Harmanpreet Kaur and Smriti Mandhana became household names. In 2022 the Indian cricket board announced equal match fees for men and women playing for India. In 2023 the Women's Premier League began, paying women cricketers far more than before.

Mithali received the Arjuna Award in 2003 and the Padma Shri in 2015. In 2021 she was given the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna, India's highest sports award. She retired from international cricket in June 2022.

The same year, a film about her life, *Shabaash Mithu*, came out. Her career also connects two eras: when she started, women cricketers often travelled in crowded second-class trains and were barely paid. When she stopped, they were signing big contracts.

Mithali never won a World Cup as a player. In November 2025 the women's team did it, beating South Africa in the final in Navi Mumbai, with Harmanpreet Kaur as captain.

Many of the players had grown up watching Mithali. Her long years at the crease helped prove that [[@womens-cricket|women's cricket]] in India deserved a big stage, and that a girl from a dance class could become a record-breaker.

text: The NBA, or National Basketball Association, is the top professional basketball league in the world. It has 30 teams, 29 in the USA and one, the Toronto Raptors, in Canada. Each team plays 82 games in the regular season, from October to April. The best teams then play knockout rounds, ending in the NBA Finals in June.
The NBA is famous for its stars, its fast, high-scoring games and its global reach. Its games are shown in more than 200 countries, and players from Europe, Africa and Asia now star in it.

Taller baskets

st.reveal: In 1950 one game finished 19–18, because a team just held the ball. In 1954 the NBA added a 24-second shot clock, so teams had to shoot quickly. Scoring jumped and games became much more exciting.

sec.h: From peach baskets to a league
sec.t:
Basketball was invented in December 1891 by James Naismith, a teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts. He needed an indoor game for students during the winter. He nailed two peach baskets to a balcony and wrote 13 rules. Someone had to climb up to get the ball out after each basket.

The league that became the NBA started in 1946 as the Basketball Association of America. In 1949 it joined with a rival league and took the name NBA. Early teams played in small arenas and some went bust within a few seasons. Black players were first allowed in 1950, when Earl Lloyd, Chuck Cooper and Nat Clifton joined NBA teams.

Some numbers in the NBA seem impossible. On 2 March 1962 Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points in one game. The Boston Celtics won 11 titles in 13 seasons between 1957 and 1969, led by Bill Russell. [[@michael-jordan|Michael Jordan]] won six titles with the [[@chicago|Chicago]] Bulls in the 1990s and has the highest career scoring average.

In 2023 LeBron James passed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar to become the league's all-time top scorer. In 2024 he became the first player to reach 40,000 points.

The basket is 3.05 metres high, the same as in Naismith's day. Most NBA players are [[@body-height-limit|very tall]], often around 2 metres. Some are taller than 2.2 metres. Height helps with reaching the basket and blocking shots. Victor Wembanyama of France, who joined the league in 2023, is about 2.2 metres tall and can still dribble like a much smaller player.

But speed, skill and vision matter too. Muggsy Bogues was about 1.60 metres tall and played 14 seasons. Many of the best passers have been some of the shorter players on the court.

Basketball is growing in India, especially in schools and cities. In 2015 the Dallas Mavericks drafted Satnam Singh Bhamara, the first player born and raised in India to be picked in the NBA draft. That same year, Sim Bhullar, a Canadian of Indian descent, became the first player of Indian heritage to play in an NBA game.

The NBA has run training programmes and an academy in India, and has played pre-season games in Mumbai. Many Indian children now know NBA players by name, wear their [[@sneakers|sneakers]] and practise their moves on local courts.

text: Viswanathan Anand is a [[@pop-chess-pieces|chess]] player from Chennai and one of the strongest players in history. In 1988 he became India's first grandmaster, the highest title in chess. He was world champion in 2000 and again from 2007 to 2013, winning the title in a knockout event, a [[tournament|tournament]] and three one-to-one matches.

Before Anand, chess in India was mostly a hobby. After him, it became a sport that children could dream about. India now has dozens of [[grandmaster|grandmasters]], and many say they started playing because of "Vishy".

st.reveal: His mother, Sushila, taught him the moves and kept encouraging him. When the family lived in Manila for a while, she copied down chess puzzles from a TV show so the two of them could solve them together.

Nobody can. There are more possible chess games than atoms in the known universe. Strong players recognise patterns from experience and look deeply only at a few promising moves.

sec.t:
Anand learnt chess from his mother, Sushila, when he was about six. As a boy he lived for a time in Manila in [[@world-philippines|the Philippines]], where his father worked, and he and his mother solved chess puzzles from a TV programme together.

Back in [[@chennai|Chennai]] he played at the Tal Chess Club and became famous for moving very fast. Opponents would still be thinking when he had already played. People called him the "Lightning Kid". In 1987 he became the first Indian to win the World Junior Championship. A year later he was a grandmaster.

Anand first became world champion in 2000, winning a knockout event that ended in Tehran. In 2007 he won the world championship tournament in Mexico City. Then he proved himself in head-to-head matches, beating Vladimir Kramnik of Russia in 2008, Veselin Topalov of Bulgaria in 2010 and Boris Gelfand of Israel in 2012.

He was known for deep preparation. His team would study openings, the first moves of a game, for months, and surprise opponents with new ideas. Anand was also one of the first top players to use [[@computers-how|computers]] heavily in his preparation. Chess programs could check his ideas for mistakes far faster than any human helper.

He is also known as one of the friendliest champions. In a sport where rivals sometimes refuse to shake hands, Anand stayed polite and calm, even after painful defeats.

{{story:memory}}

In April 2010, Anand was in Germany, about to fly to Sofia, Bulgaria, for his match against Topalov. Then the Eyjafjallajökull volcano in [[@iceland|Iceland]] erupted. Its ash cloud closed airports across Europe.

Anand and his team set off by road, a journey of about 40 hours through several countries. He asked for a short delay, but the organisers allowed only one day. He lost the first game, tired from the trip, but won the match.

In 2013 Anand defended his title in his home city, Chennai, against the young Norwegian Magnus Carlsen. Carlsen won clearly and became champion. Anand challenged him again in 2014 and lost again. He said later that losing to Carlsen was painful, but that the younger man was simply better at that time.

Anand kept playing at the top level for years and won the World Rapid Championship in 2017, aged 48.

India's chess boom is often called the Anand effect. India had just one grandmaster in 1988 and more than 80 by 2024. In December 2024 Gukesh Dommaraju of Chennai, then 18, became the youngest undisputed world champion in history. Anand had helped train him at his academy.

The same year India won both the open and women's gold medals at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest. Anand himself has become a coach, commentator and an official of FIDE, the world chess federation. He received the Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian award, in 2007.

text: The Holocaust was the murder of about six million Jewish men, women and children by Nazi Germany and those who helped it, during the Second World War. It is one of the worst crimes in human history. The word [[holocaust|holocaust]] comes from an ancient Greek word for a sacrifice that was completely burned. Many Jewish people use the Hebrew word *Shoah*, meaning catastrophe.

Before the war, Europe was home to about nine and a half million Jewish people. By 1945, about two out of every three of them had been murdered. Whole communities, with their schools, songs and ways of life, disappeared.

The Nazis also killed many others they saw as enemies or "unworthy", including Roma people, disabled people, Polish and Soviet civilians, prisoners of war and gay men. Historians know a great deal about how it happened, because the Nazis kept records, and survivors told what they saw.

st.prompt: In 1939 a ship called the St. Louis carried more than 900 Jewish refugees from Germany. What happened when it reached Cuba and then the United States?

options.t: They were welcomed and given homes
They were turned away and the ship sailed back to Europe

st.reveal: Cuba, the United States and Canada all refused to let most passengers land. Other European countries took them in, but many of those places were later conquered by Germany, and about 250 of the passengers were killed in the Holocaust.

myth: Jewish people did not fight back during the Holocaust.

Many resisted, in many ways. In 1943 Jews in the Warsaw Ghetto rose up and held off German troops for about a month. Others escaped to join resistance fighters in the forests, hid children, or secretly kept records so the truth would survive.

sec.t:
Adolf Hitler and his Nazi party came to power in Germany in 1933. They blamed Jewish people for Germany's problems, using lies that spread through newspapers, films and school lessons. This kind of [[@propaganda|propaganda]] made cruelty seem normal to many people.

Step by step, Jewish Germans lost their rights. In 1935 new laws took away their citizenship. They were pushed out of jobs and schools. In November 1938, in a night of attacks later called Kristallnacht, synagogues were burned and Jewish shops smashed across Germany and Austria. Many families tried to leave, but other countries took in only some of them.

Some people risked their lives to save others. In Denmark, ordinary people helped about 7,000 Jews escape by boat to Sweden in 1943. Before the war, a rescue effort called the Kindertransport carried about 10,000 Jewish children to safety in Britain. Many never saw their parents again.

In 1940 a Japanese diplomat in Lithuania, Chiune Sugihara, went against his own government's orders. For about six weeks he wrote travel visas by hand, sometimes for hours a day, so that Jewish [[refugee|refugees]] could cross Russia and Japan to safety. His visas are thought to have saved thousands of people, and many of their [[descendant|descendants]] are alive today.

Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem, honours rescuers as "Righteous Among the Nations". More than 28,000 people have been recognised so far.

Allied soldiers freed the camps in 1945 and were shocked by what they found. Leading Nazis were put on trial at Nuremberg in Germany, one of the first times a country's leaders faced an international court for crimes against humanity.

The horror helped push the world to write the Universal Declaration of [[@human-rights|Human Rights]] in 1948. Survivors spent the rest of their lives telling their stories, so that nobody could deny what happened. Today, museums such as the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C., and the Anne Frank House in [[@amsterdam|Amsterdam]] keep those memories alive. It can be a heavy subject, and it helps to talk about it with a parent or teacher.

text: Angkor was built by the Khmer, the people of Cambodia. From about 802 CE to the 1400s, their kings ruled a powerful [[empire|empire]] across much of South-East Asia, covering parts of today's Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and Vietnam.

Their capital, Angkor, grew into one of the largest cities in the world before modern times. Its kings built hundreds of stone temples there. The most famous is [[@angkor-wat|Angkor Wat]], built in the early 1100s by King Suryavarman II.
Angkor Wat was first a Hindu temple to the god Vishnu. Later it became a Buddhist temple, which it still is. It is so important to Cambodians that it appears on the national flag.

st.prompt: How did the people of Angkor keep rice growing through the long dry season?

options.t: They built huge reservoirs and canals to store monsoon rain
They carried water from the sea in clay pots
They only grew rice in years with no dry season

st.reveal: The Khmer dug enormous rectangular reservoirs called barays, some about 8 km long, and a web of canals. These stored and moved water from the monsoon so fields could be watered for much of the year.

sec.t:
Long before Angkor, traders and priests from India sailed to South-East Asia. They brought Sanskrit, Hindu gods and Buddhist teachings, and stories like the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the Mahabharata. Local rulers blended these ideas with their own traditions.

So Khmer kings took Sanskrit names ending in "varman", meaning protector. Their temples were built as mountains for the gods, like Mount Meru in Hindu and Buddhist stories, the centre of the universe. The walls of Angkor Wat are carved with Hindu scenes, including the gods and demons churning the ocean of milk.

Angkor Wat covers a huge area. A moat about 190 m wide surrounds it, so wide it looks like a lake. A long stone causeway crosses the moat to the gates. Inside, galleries and courtyards rise towards five tall towers shaped like lotus buds.

The builders used sandstone from quarries in the Kulen hills, about 40 km away. Blocks were probably floated along canals on rafts. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] estimate that several million blocks were used, some weighing over a tonne. They were cut to fit together tightly, often without mortar.

The walls are covered with carvings. One gallery alone has carved panels hundreds of metres long showing battles, gods and the king himself.

{{story:monsoon}}

Angkor depended on water. The [[monsoon|monsoon]] brought heavy rain for part of the year, then months of dry weather. To keep rice growing, the Khmer dug a vast system of canals and giant [[reservoir|reservoirs]] called barays. The largest, the West Baray, is about 8 km long and over 2 km wide.

In 2012 and 2015, scientists used lidar, a way of mapping with [[@lasers|lasers]] fired from aircraft, to see through the forest. They found the faint outlines of streets, houses, ponds and fields spreading for many kilometres around the temples. Angkor had been far bigger than anyone thought.

Around 1181 King Jayavarman VII came to power. He was a Buddhist, and he built a new walled city, Angkor Thom. At its heart is the Bayon temple, with more than 200 huge calm stone faces gazing in every direction.

He also built roads, rest houses and hospitals across the empire. Another of his temples, Ta Prohm, has been left partly wrapped in the roots of giant trees, which makes it one of the most photographed places in Asia.

From the 1300s, the Khmer Empire grew weaker. Wars with the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya, changes in trade, and long [[drought|droughts]] followed by floods that damaged the canals all probably played a part. By the 1400s the capital had moved south, towards Phnom Penh.

Monks kept worshipping at Angkor Wat. In the 1860s the writings of a French traveller, Henri Mouhot, made it famous in Europe. Since then many countries have helped repair the temples. From 1986 to 1993, experts from the Archaeological Survey of India worked on cleaning and strengthening Angkor Wat. Today crowds of visitors from around the world walk its causeway at dawn to watch the sun rise behind the towers.

text: Qin Shi Huang was the first emperor to unite China, in 221 BCE. He was powerful and fearful of death. He built a vast tomb near the modern city of Xi'an and filled pits nearby with an army of about 8,000 clay soldiers, with horses, chariots and real bronze weapons.

Many people in ancient China believed that life continued after death, and that a ruler would need servants, officials and protectors there too. The clay army was meant to guard the emperor and help him rule in the afterlife. It was forgotten for more than 2,000 years, until farmers found it by accident in 1974.

st.prompt: Why hasn't the emperor's own burial chamber been opened?

options.t: Archaeologists fear damaging what's inside and can't yet protect it
Nobody knows where it is
It's full of water

st.reveal: Experts know where the tomb mound is, but opening it could destroy fragile paint, silk and wood within moments. An ancient historian also wrote about rivers of mercury inside, and soil tests have found high mercury levels. China has decided to wait for better technology.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor.
Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, Xi'an.
Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji).
n.certNote: The army's purpose is widely agreed, to serve the emperor after death, but the total number of figures is an estimate because much of the site is still unexcavated, and the emperor's own tomb has never been opened.

myth: The Terracotta Army was always grey or brown, like it looks today.

The soldiers were brightly painted in reds, greens, blues, purples and pinks. Most of the paint flaked off over time, and when figures are dug up, remaining paint can peel away within minutes as it dries.
